en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Buddha, Concerning the Question on Inference.
9. The Question on Water, Sentient Beings, and Life “Venerable Nāgasena, when this water is being heated over a fire, it makes various sounds—*cicciṭāyati*, *ciṭiciṭāyati*.
Venerable Nāgasena, does water possess life? What living thing is it that makes these sounds while playing?”
“Or does it sound because it is being crushed by something else?

“No, Great King, water does not live; there is no life or sentient being in water. However, Great King, due to the great intensity of the heat of the fire, the water hisses, crackles, and makes various kinds of sounds.
“Venerable Nāgasena, here certain sectarians, claiming that water lives, reject cold water and [use] hot water...”
“Having heated it, they consume it one by one in private, and they reproach and despise you, saying:
‘The recluses, sons of the Sakyans, destroy a single-sensed life. Therefore, dispel, remove, and drive away that reproach and contempt.

“No indeed, Great King, water does not live; there is no life or being in water, Great King. However, Great King, due to the great intensity of the heat from the fire, the water hisses, sizzles, and makes various sounds.”

“Great King, suppose water from pools, lakes, rivers, streams, ponds, caves, marshes, wells, low-lying places, and lotus-pools were to be exhausted and depleted due to the great force of wind and heat;

would that water there sizzle, hiss, or make various kinds of sounds? “No, indeed not, venerable sir. “In the same way, Great King, when a person’s body is consumed by the great heat of fever, does it sizzle, hiss, or make various kinds of sounds? “No, indeed not, venerable sir. “In the same way, Great King, when a person’s body is consumed by the great heat of fever, it does not sizzle, hiss, or make various kinds of sounds. Yet, Great King, the fire-element within the body is still present; it is simply that it is overcome by the other elements and cannot manifest its own specific function.”
“No indeed, Bhante.
“If, Great King, water were alive, it would also make a sound there. For this reason too, Great King, you should know:
‘There is no life or being in water; it is because of the great intensity of the heat of the fire that the water hisses.’”
"It crackles and makes many kinds of sounds.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another further reason: "There is no life or being in water; it is because of the great intensity of the heat of the fire that the water makes a sound.
But when, Great King, water mixed with rice is placed in a vessel, covered, and set on the stove, does the water make a sound there?"
“Certainly not, venerable sir; it is still and motionless.
“But then, great king, suppose that very same water were placed on a hearth after a fire had been lit in a vessel—would the water there be still and motionless?

“Certainly not, venerable sir; it would move, it would churn, it would boil, it would become turbid; it would be whipped up with waves, it would go upward, downward, and in every direction, it would overflow, it would splash about, and it would be covered with a mass of foam.”
“But why, Great King, does that ordinary water not move but remains still; and why, when it has reached fire,
does it move, churn, boil, become turbid, break into waves, go upward, downward, and in all directions, overflow, splash about,
and become covered with a garland of foam?”
“Venerable sir, ordinary water does not move; however, water that has been heated by fire hisses, sizzles, and makes various kinds of sounds because of the great intensity of the heat from the fire.
“For this reason also, Great King, you should know: ‘There is no living being or creature in water; it is the great intensity of the heat from the fire that causes the water to sound.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another superior reason why there is no living being or creature in water, and why the water sounds due to the great intensity of the heat from the fire.
“Is that water, Great King, present in every house, contained in water-jars, and covered?
“Yes, venerable sir.

“But does that water, Great King, move, stir, churn, become turbid, break into waves, go upward, downward, or in the cardinal and intermediate directions, overflow, splash about, and form a mass of foam?”
“Certainly not, venerable sir; that water contained in a water-jar remains unmoving and natural.
“But have you ever heard, Great King, that the water in the great ocean moves, stirs, churns, becomes turbid, and is filled with waves;
that it goes upward, downward, and in all directions and intermediate directions; that it surges, leaps over, and becomes garlanded with foam?”
“Does it rise up, fall back, strike against the shore, and make a great variety of sounds?
“Yes, venerable sir, I have heard this before and I have seen it: that the water in the great ocean rises up into the sky by a hundred cubits, even two hundred cubits.
“For what reason, Great King, does the water contained in a water-jar neither move nor make a sound, while the water in the great ocean moves and makes a sound?”

“Venerable sir, because of the great force of the wind, the water in the great ocean moves and makes a sound; but water contained in a water-pot does not move nor make a sound unless it is struck by something.
“Great king, just as the water in the great ocean moves and makes a sound because of the great force of the wind, even so the water makes a sound because of the great force of the heat of the fire.”
“Is it not the case, great king, that they bind a dry drumhead with dry ox-hide?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“But does a drum have a soul or a sentient being, great king?”
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“But why, great king, does the drum resound?
“Because of the effort applied by a woman or a man, venerable sir.”
“Just as, Great King, a drum resounds through the appropriate effort of a woman or a man, even so water resounds due to the great intensity of the heat of fire.
By this reason also, Great King, you should know: ‘There is no life-principle or being in water; water resounds due to the great intensity of the heat of fire.’”
"Great King, I too have something to ask of you, so that this question may be thoroughly resolved:
Great King, when water is being heated in all the vessels, does it make a sound,
or does it make a sound only in some of the vessels?"
“Certainly not, venerable sir; water being heated does not make a sound with all vessels alike, but only with certain vessels.
“In that case, Great King, you have abandoned your own doctrine and returned to my position: there is no living being or soul in water.
If, Great King, water being heated were to make a sound with all vessels alike, then it would be appropriate to say, ‘Water lives.’”
For water, Great King, does not become twofold such that "that which makes a sound lives, and that which does not make a sound does not live. If, Great King, water were alive,
then when great elephant-kings with massive bodies and broken temples draw it up with their trunks,
put it into their mouths, and cause it to enter their bellies— that water would remain between their tusks.
Being pressed down, it would make a sound.

Even great ships a hundred cubits long, heavy and burdensome, filled with many hundreds of thousands of loads, as they travel upon the great ocean—even when the water is pressed down by them—it would make a sound.
Furthermore, there are very large fish with bodies many hundreds of yojanas long—timis, timingalas, timirapiṅgalas—within [the depths].
“Submerged in the great ocean, dwelling there as their place of residence, they drink and belch forth great torrents of water;
even for them, that water being squeezed between their teeth or in their bellies would make a sound.

Yet, Great King, because water being thus oppressed by such and such great oppressions does not make a sound, for this reason too there is no life or being in water. Thus, Great King, you should hold it.”
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! This question, which had come with fault, has been resolved by a fitting analysis.

Just as, venerable Nāgasena, a precious gem-stone, having reached a skilled, expert, and well-trained lapidary, would receive fame, praise, and commendation; or as a pearl-jewel or a fine cloth-jewel [would do so].”
“Or as a cloth-seller, or as one who has obtained red sandalwood or perfumes, might gain fame, praise, and commendation.
Even so, venerable Nāgasena, this question, having been brought forward with fault, has been analyzed with a fitting analysis; thus it is, and I accept it as such.
This is the ninth question concerning water, sentient beings, and life.
The first chapter is the Buddhavagga.
In this chapter there are nine questions.
